questions.prompt: A study links health classes attended with health quiz score. Which choice best separates the two measures from a fair starting condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Compare the first measure, record the second, and match starting conditions.

options.label: B
options.text: Compare the second measure and ignore starting conditions.

options.label: C
options.text: Use the first measure as both the factor and the result.

options.label: D
options.text: Use different starting conditions to make any effect larger.

support.hint: Identify the factor being compared, the outcome being measured, and what should be similar before the comparison.

stuck.introduction: Separate the study's measures from its starting conditions.
steps: Ask which recorded measure represents exposure to the health classes.
Ask which recorded measure represents the outcome the study wants to explain.
Check whether an option compares the factor and outcome while accounting for relevant differences that existed before the classes.

questions.prompt: At a clinic, what changes when people have similar starting scores?

options.label: A
options.text: The numbers prove the program causes a two-point loss for everyone.

options.label: B
options.text: The program is lower in both matched groups; overall means may mislead.

options.label: C
options.text: The program is better for every group because 85 is above 75.

options.label: D
options.text: Matching starting scores removes the need to compare results.

support.hint: Read the comparisons within similar starting-score groups as well as the overall comparison.

stuck.introduction: Compare like starting conditions before judging the overall pattern.
steps: Record the overall Program and Other means without treating that comparison as a causal conclusion.
Compare Program with Other separately within the low-starting-score group and the high-starting-score group.
Check which statement respects all three comparisons and avoids claiming an effect for every individual.
